title: MBA Graduates Now Earn 52% More Than Engineers in India, and the Gap Is Widening
excerpt: Deloitte India's Campus Workforce Trends 2026 report shows management roles commanding a growing salary premium over engineering positions, with the gap projected to hit 59% next year.
body:
• MBA graduates in India's 2026 campus placements earned average salaries 52% higher than engineering graduates, according to Deloitte India's Campus Workforce Trends 2026 report.
  • The premium is projected to widen to 59% for the 2026-27 placement cycle, up from 47% for the class of 2025.
  • Top 10 business schools offered average annual compensation of ₹27.4 lakh ($33,000), more than 3.3 times the ₹8.4 lakh average at tier-3 institutions.
  • All 250 surveyed employers said they now place greater value on management-oriented roles over purely technical positions.

The Management Premium

MBA graduates are pulling further ahead of their engineering counterparts in India's campus hiring market, with management roles commanding a 52% salary premium over engineering positions in 2026 placements, according to Deloitte India's Campus Workforce Trends 2026 report.

That gap is widening. For the class of 2025, the premium stood at 47%. For the upcoming 2026-27 placement cycle, Deloitte projects it will reach 59% — a trend that points to a structural shift in what corporate India is willing to pay for.

The report surveyed 250 organizations across 505 nationally ranked institutions. Every single employer reported placing greater value on management-oriented and leadership talent over purely technical roles.

"The recruiters are emphasizing professionals who can translate technology into business outcomes."

— Neelesh Gupta, Partner, Deloitte India

What Is Driving the Shift

The premium reflects a fundamental change in hiring priorities. Companies are no longer simply filling technical seats — they want professionals who can combine digital and analytical capabilities with commercial understanding and strategic decision-making.

Neelesh Gupta, a partner at Deloitte India, said the demand is for talent that can turn technological advances into concrete business results. The shift has accelerated as AI transforms business operations, creating demand for leaders who understand both the technology and its commercial applications.

A separate analysis by The Hindu Business Line found that supply-chain specialists, procurement experts, and AI-linked operational managers are commanding salary premiums of 30-40% over traditional generalist MBA roles. Companies are increasingly rewarding "deployment-ready MBAs" — graduates who arrive with demonstrable AI and operational project experience rather than relying solely on academic pedigree.

The Tier Divide

The salary data reveals stark differences across institutions. Deloitte found that the average annual compensation at India's top 10 business schools stood at ₹27.4 lakh (approximately $33,000), compared with ₹8.4 lakh at tier-3 business schools — a gap of more than 3.3 times within the same degree category.

Top-tier institutions like ISB Hyderabad reported an 11% increase in average compensation to ₹37.29 lakh, while SPJIMR placed its largest-ever batch of 356 students at an average package of ₹33.75 lakh, according to The Hindu Business Line.

The tier-1 MBA category extends beyond the IIMs to include management schools at IIT Bombay, IIT Madras, and IIT Kharagpur, as well as private institutions like SP Jain and IMI Delhi.

The Fine Print: Bigger CTCs, Less Certainty

Beneath the headline salary growth, compensation structures are changing. Variable pay now accounts for 30-40% of packages in several sectors, up sharply from roughly 15-20% until recently. Joining bonuses and relocation allowances are shrinking.

AI-native startups, agentic workflow firms, and fintech platforms are recruiting aggressively alongside traditional consulting and BFSI firms, often offering equity-led compensation that inflates headline CTC figures. Recruiters describe this as the "fat CTC" phenomenon — larger packages with weaker income certainty.

Companies are also expanding internship-to-hire programs and using AI more extensively in recruitment as they compete for candidates with digital and analytical skills.

What This Means for Diaspora Professionals

For Indian-origin professionals in the US and elsewhere weighing an MBA, the data underscores a widening opportunity in India's corporate market — but context matters. The 52% premium reflects campus placement averages across surveyed institutions, not a guarantee for any individual graduate. College tier, specialization, and the specific employer matter more than the degree name alone.

The broader signal is clear: corporate India is restructuring around technology-meets-business talent, and that demand is reshaping compensation across the board.
